hops.afterHeading: Two answers, and what each predicts
hops.title: Mice bred for extra whiskers grew extra barrels
hops.text: In 1977 Hendrik Van der Loos and his colleagues began breeding twenty-one ordinary lab mice for stray extra whiskers. They ended up with thirteen strains with matching left and right whisker patterns, twelve of them bred for extras. In the barrel field, wherever they checked, an extra whisker almost always had its own barrel in the matching spot on the map. A closer study of six strains found that a whisker needed enough sensory nerve fibers to earn a barrel, and that within each strain, barrel area rose in line with fiber count. The snout, not only the sheet, gets a say in what the cortex builds.

sources.citation: Van der Loos H, Welker E, Dorfl J & Rumo G. Selective breeding for variations in patterns of mystacial vibrissae of mice. J. Hered. 77:66 (1986).
Welker E & Van der Loos H. Quantitative correlation between barrel-field size and the sensory innervation of the whiskerpad. J. Neurosci. 6:3355 (1986).

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A white mouse with extra whiskers sitting next to a brass microscope on a wooden workbench.
image.caption: Mice bred for extra whiskers usually built a matching extra barrel in cortex for each well-supplied whisker.

hops.afterHeading: A lamp at the front: FGF8
hops.title: Blind cavefish switch on FGF8 two hours early
hops.text: The Mexican tetra comes in two forms: a sighted surface fish and a blind cave fish. Pachón cavefish embryos start to build eyes with a much reduced or missing lower retina, and the eyes later degenerate as lens cells die. In those embryos, forebrain FGF8 switches on about two hours earlier than in surface fish. A patch of early neural plate that helps build the lower retina in surface fish mostly becomes hypothalamus in cavefish. Blocking FGF receptors in young cavefish embryos moved gene expression back toward the surface-fish pattern. The authors argue that this early start is a key timing change behind that loss of lower retina.

sources.citation: Pottin K, Hinaux H & Retaux S. Restoring eye size in Astyanax mexicanus blind cavefish embryos through modulation of the Shh and Fgf8 forebrain organising centres. Development 138:2467 (2011).

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A pale eyeless cavefish swimming beside a silvery sighted tetra in a rocky cave pool.
image.caption: In Pachón cavefish embryos, forebrain FGF8 starts about two hours early; the authors propose this shifts lower-retina fate toward hypothalamus.

hops.title: Visual cortex does not sit idle in blind people
hops.text: What does visual cortex do after loss of sight? In PET scans, primary visual cortex became active when early-blind volunteers read Braille; on other touch-discrimination tasks it switched on in blind volunteers but quieted in sighted ones. Brief magnetic pulses over occipital cortex made early-blind readers stumble on Braille and raised letters; sighted volunteers feeling raised letters were unaffected. In 2011, two expert echolocators who hike and mountain bike using mouth clicks, one blind since infancy, one since fourteen, heard matched click recordings with and without echoes in a scanner. Visual cortex responded to echoes, with no detectable difference in auditory cortex. Territory sketched for sight can serve other senses.

sources.citation: Sadato N et al. Activation of the primary visual cortex by Braille reading in blind subjects. Nature 380:526 (1996).
Cohen LG et al. Functional relevance of cross-modal plasticity in blind humans. Nature 389:180 (1997).
Thaler L, Arnott SR & Goodale MA. Neural correlates of natural human echolocation in early and late blind echolocation experts. PLoS ONE 6:e20162 (2011).

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: Hands reading an open Braille book on a table beside a mountain bike leaning against a sunny brick wall.
image.caption: Occipital cortex helps early-blind readers read Braille and responds to echoes in blind echolocation experts.

audio.title: Teeth, area size and sound in visual cortex
audio.transcript:
In a textbook, a mouse cortex looks tidy: motor at the front, touch in the middle, vision at the back. Real brains are less tidy than that, and the borders turn out to be more negotiable than the diagram suggests. Here are three true stories about how cortex divides up its surface.

The first is the naked mole-rat, a hairless rodent that lives underground. Its oversized front teeth stick permanently outside its mouth, and it uses them for digging, handling objects, social interactions and feeding. In two thousand two, Kenneth Catania and Michael Remple mapped the touch cortex of these animals. Nearly one third of primary somatosensory cortex, thirty-one percent, was devoted to the upper and lower front teeth. And the touch area as a whole is so enlarged, as a share of the neocortex, that it covers virtually all of the cortex that is devoted to vision in a laboratory rat. For an animal that digs and handles things with its teeth, touch won the land grab.

The second story asks whether the exact size of an area matters. In two thousand seven, Axel Leingartner, Dennis O'Leary and colleagues raised the level of E M X two in the cortical progenitors of mouse embryos. Just as the gradient rule predicts, the motor area at the front and the touch area nearer the middle both shrank, and as adults these mice did worse on touch and movement tasks. You might guess that the reverse, lowering E M X two so that those areas grow larger, would make a mouse unusually deft. It did not. Mice with larger touch and motor areas also did worse on tests that challenged their balance and coordination. When the team used genetic crosses to bring cortical E M X two back to normal, the areas moved back toward their usual sizes, and the mice performed about as well as ordinary mice. Bigger is not simply better. An area seems to have a right size.

The third story goes underground again, to a different animal: the blind mole-rat, Spalax ehrenbergi. It is blind, and its eyes are tiny, yet under the microscope the back of its cortex still has the structure of a typical mammal's primary visual cortex. So what is that cortex doing? In two thousand two, Gilles Bronchti and colleagues showed that sounds activate it. Most of that auditory input arrives through the thalamic relay that normally carries vision, the dorsal lateral geniculate nucleus, which in this animal receives input from the inferior colliculus, a station on the hearing pathway. It is the rewired ferret run in reverse, and nature did the rewiring.

Put the three together and the lesson's rule holds up from an unexpected angle. Genes in the embryonic sheet sketch the map, but how an animal lives, and what input arrives, decide a great deal about what each patch of cortex ends up doing.
